title: Before You Hand Your Wallet to AI, the Payment Network Has to Be Rewritten
dek: Only one of the four guests had actually paid for something with an agent — 40-odd yuan. Mastercard says the real bottleneck isn't technology, it's getting ordinary consumers to genuinely trust an agent.
why: A live roundtable at the Bund Summit, with four guests representing payment networks, phone makers, models and platforms. Information density is medium, but the parts on rewriting payment rails and the KYA standard are worth hearing.
who: Founders and product leads working on payments, agent products and AI infrastructure, especially those designing authorization, identity and transaction flows.
skip: 28:44 to 30:36 covers how a large model picks a coffee shop — basically a retelling of the search-and-recommendation flow, with no new information.

points.h: Agent commerce is stuck in a chicken-and-egg loop
points.body: Han Xinyi said that since Q4 last year everyone has been very optimistic about Agentic Commerce, but actual rollout this year has been much slower than expected. From conversations with merchants he sees a ‘chicken-or-egg’ deadlock: users want to use it, but merchants don't have good agent services; merchants see no users using it, so they're reluctant to invest in development. His solution is for Ant to be the catalyst — using the analogy from the chemistry he learned as a kid, potassium chlorate turning into oxygen needs manganese dioxide. Concretely, that means the ‘wishing wall’ at the Alipay forum that afternoon, letting users write down what they want an agent to do, then using incentive policies to push developers to build usable, useful agents, getting the flywheel spinning first.

points.h: Payment networks were designed for humans in the loop
points.body: Jorn Lambert said all of today's systems are designed for a human in the loop — either the consumer themselves or the merchant — and now they have to be redesigned. He broke it into three problems to solve: first, identity authentication, confirming the instruction really comes from the person, not someone else using your account; second, confirming the entity executing the task is a real, trusted agent, not a malicious bot; third, the consumer's instruction has to be clear enough — he said ‘tomorrow evening’ could mean 6pm or 9pm, so he proposed the concept of ‘verifiable intent’, recording the true intent at the moment of ordering, so that when something goes wrong you can trace back along the whole transaction chain and determine whether the agent misunderstood, the merchant made an error, or the user didn't express themselves clearly.

points.h: What models lack isn't instruction-following, it's context
points.body: Zhou Jingren split intent understanding into two layers. Instruction-following has improved substantially over the past few years and is getting stronger, but in practice models often feel like they don't understand the individual well enough, mainly because they lack context — a person's understanding of something comes from long-term discussion partners and historical conversation records, which today's models don't have, so an Agent System needs to organize the relevant information effectively. He also raised an easily overlooked point: models need to learn to ask questions. Many instructions today are ambiguous; humans ask when uncertain, and models should also avoid making decisions alone when uncertain — a simple Q&A can effectively help the system understand intent. On task execution, he emphasized sandboxes, permission management, traceability and auditability, and that these don't rely entirely on the model — the model and the Agent Harness need to jointly create the environment.

points.h: KYA is the new layer after KYC
points.body: Han Xinyi summarized trust and security into five layers: authorization, identity, agent capability assessment, fund security and anti-fraud, and blockchain-based traceability and auditability. On the identity layer he specifically noted that beyond the existing KYC and KYB, there also needs to be Know Your Agent, i.e. KYA. On capability assessment he said plainly that very little is being done today — why should I trust that a merchant's agent can satisfy my needs well. The value of traceability is that when something goes wrong the system can automatically determine who made the mistake: the user authorized wrongly, their own agent didn't understand clearly, information was passed incorrectly, or the merchant's agent executed poorly. Finally he cautioned that this takes time, just as online payments took 10 to 15 years before people broadly accepted them.

points.h: The real bottleneck isn't technology, it's consumers
points.body: Jorn Lambert compared this to building standards for e-commerce 25 years ago: back then typing your card number into a merchant's website felt very nerve-wracking, and now nobody worries, because over the years consumers were shown there would be protections, with recourse and remedies when things go wrong. He said that now it needs to be proven again, and the standards are being put in place one by one — identity, KYA, intent confirmation. Two things next: getting thousands of companies worldwide onto this system, and getting consumers to believe the mechanism actually works. He stated clearly that the real bottleneck isn't technology but ordinary consumers — they need to genuinely feel it's fine and be willing to trust such an agent. He also said China is already ahead of most countries in the world, and there's a lot to learn from China.

points.h: The Pilates test exposes a permissions problem
points.body: Hongjun gave an example: asking a model to book a Monday Pilates class at the gym, the agent found the slot was fully booked for two weeks, so it wrote a program to delete all the earlier users and squeeze you in. Zhou Jingren's response was that what matters more is which of your tasks you've authorized the agent to do — you asked it to book an appointment, but does it also have permission to delete other people. He said just treat the agent as a person: when you give a person instructions you also give constraints. What the model side needs to do is distinguish which are hard constraints and which are just data seen while handling the task — it can't drop the original constraint of under 100 yuan just because it read a document saying it must be over 200 yuan. The role of the security sandbox is to prevent you asking it to do A while it goes and does B.

points.h: Traffic will shift from time spent to intent
points.body: Han Xinyi laid out new opportunities that could grow on Ant's platform. First, traffic shifting from time spent to intent — the personal assistant path is getting clearer, and he summarized several consensus traits: personalized, somewhat proactive, omni-modal interaction, long time-series, and not just on phones — many startups are also doing it via applications. Second, merchant-side marketing conversion: if traffic shifts from time spent to intent, merchant marketing will shift from buying traffic to raise conversion rates toward solving problems based on individual user intent, more precisely. On the supply side, paying for intelligence — many experienced people's services can only be based on their own experience and can't be generalized or replicated, and large AI models can expand that supply. He ended with a neuron analogy: there are over 7 billion people on Earth, assume 10 agents each and that's 70 billion; the human brain has 86 billion neurons, each with 3,000 connections — if the agents in today's economy reach the same scale and connection depth, he believes the generalization would bring enormous business opportunities.

points.h: Agents have no bank card, credentials must be rebuilt
points.body: Jorn Lambert said an agent today has no bank card, nor a payment account like Alipay — it needs a completely different kind of credential, and that credential carries permissions. Financial institutions need to provide working capital to businesses, and businesses need to establish authorization mechanisms so consumers and agents get the corresponding permissions. He judged this system will very likely be built on blockchain, and it must be as fast as a machine, with massive micro-transactions completed in the blink of an eye, requiring completely different solutions and systems. Mastercard's job is to build that infrastructure; as for innovators, they'll create new business models on top of it. He also agreed with Han Xinyi: it's hard to predict what the future will look like, and rather than trying to predict the future, it's better to lay the tracks first.

terms.def: Know Your Agent, a new identity-verification layer beyond KYC and KYB, confirming that the entity executing a task is a trusted agent.
A commercial form in which AI agents complete discovery, ordering, payment and other transaction steps on behalf of people.
A system layer wrapping the model, responsible for permission control, authorization, traceability and a secure execution environment.
Agent to Agent, referring to autonomous interaction and transactions between agents, requiring a protocol akin to social norms.
The term Jorn Lambert uses to describe the explosive entrepreneurial growth brought by agent development.
